title: On a geometric dimension growth conjecture
speaker: Yotam Hendel
abstract:
Let X be an irreducible projective variety of degree at least 2 defined over Q, and let B>0 be an integer. The dimension growth conjecture, now proven in almost all cases following works of Browning, Heath-Brown and Salberger, provides a uniform upper bound on the number of rational points of height at most B lying on X.
 
Shifting to the geometric setting, where X may be defined over C(t), the collection of C(t)-rational points of height B lying on X is a possibly infinite set which naturally forms an algebraic variety, which we denote by X(B). In current work, we uniformly bound the dimension and, when the degree of X is at least 6, the number of irreducible components of X(B) of largest possible dimension, obtaining a geometric analogue of the dimension growth conjecture.
In order to do so, we develop a geometric version of Heath--Brown's determinant method which is of independent interest, and use results on rational points on curves over function fields. 

Joint work with Tijs Buggenhout and Floris Vermeulen.

title: Gröbner bases beyond polynomials, and what they count
speaker: Anton Khoroshkin
abstract: Gröbner bases are usually presented as a tool of computer algebra, but at heart they are a counting device. Once a Gröbner basis of an algebra is known, the algebra has a basis of “normal” monomials: those that avoid a prescribed set of forbidden patterns. Questions about dimensions and Hilbert series therefore become questions about counting pattern-avoiding objects, and conversely, avoidance problems can be attacked by algebraic means. I will start by recalling this picture for commutative and associative algebras and explain why Gröbner bases became so widespread once computers could do the work. I will then move to algebraic structures whose “monomials” are richer combinatorial objects: (bi)shuffle algebras, built from permutations and set compositions, and, time permitting, operads and contractads, whose components are indexed by graphs. Gröbner bases still make sense in these settings, and they shed light on problems such as (consecutive) pattern avoidance in permutations and the generating series of combinatorial species. I assume no prior knowledge of Gröbner bases or operads.

title: Completing large low-rank matrices from only a few (and partially corrupted) observed entries
speaker: Boaz Nadler
abstract: Suppose you observe very few entries from a large matrix. Can we predict the missing entries, say assuming the matrix is (approximately) low rank ? We describe a simple method to solve this matrix completion problem. We show our method is able to recover matrices from very few entries and/or with ill-conditioned matrices, where many other popular methods fail. Furthermore, due to its simplicity, it is easy to extend our method to related problems including 1-bit and robust matrix completion. On the theoretical front, we prove that our method enjoys some of the strongest available recovery guarantees.

title: The Lagrangian spectral distance for Clifford tori
speaker: Frol Zapolsky
location: Schreiber bldg., room 309, Tel Aviv University (and online via zoom).
abstract: Various metrics have been defined in symplectic topology on infinite-dimensional spaces such as the Hamiltonian group or the space of Lagrangian submanifolds which are Hamiltonian isotopic to a given one - the Hofer metric and its Lagrangian analog due to Chekanov, as well as metrics coming from Floer-homological spectral invariants, colloquially known as spectral distances. In this talk I'll present the following result: the space of Lagrangians which are Hamiltonian isotopic to the Clifford torus in a standard complex projective space (of complex dimension at least 2) or in the complex two-dimensional quadric (S^2 x S^2), taken with the Lagrangian spectral distance relative to suitable coefficients, contains a quasi-isometric copy of the real line, and thus in particular has infinite diameter. This also implies the same result for the Lagrangian Hofer metric for those spaces. In the case of complex projective spaces this requires coefficients in the integers or in certain finite rings which are not fields, and in the case of the quadric, coefficients in a local system of rank two.

title: Spatial Audio: Foundations and Machine Learning Challenges
speaker: Boaz Rafaely
location: Lecture Hall - Room 1 - אולם הרצאות חדר 1, Jacob Ziskind Building
abstract: Spatial audio aims to capture and reproduce acoustic scenes while preserving the listener’s sense of direction, distance, and surrounding space. This seminar will introduce the foundations of spatial audio, including microphone array recording, Ambisonics representations and encoding, and binaural reproduction over headphones. We will then examine the challenges of recording spatial sound using a small number of microphones on wearable devices, highlighting recent approaches and the importance of perceptually motivated optimization. The talk will address speech enhancement using neural networks for spatial audio, including array agnostic approaches, the estimation of higher-order Ambisonics signals from low-order recordings, and preservation of spatial hearing cues when optimizing audio reproduction.BioBoaz Rafaely is a Professor at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev in Israel, where he leads the Acoustics Laboratory, conducting research in spatial audio signal processing. He has published over 200 papers in journals and conferences, and is the author of the book Fundamentals of Spherical Array Processing. Prof. Rafaely has previously served as Head of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at BGU, Chair of the Israeli Acoustical Association, and Chair of the Technical Committee on Audio Signal Processing of the European Acoustical Association. He has also been an associate editor for IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing, IEEE Signal Processing Letters, and Acta Acustica. He is an IEEE fellow

title: From Molecules to Macroscopic Devices: Advanced Carbon Nanotube Hybrids for Energy Applications
speaker: Haim Weissman
department: 2026-2027 Spotlight on Science Seminar Series - Dr. Haim Weissman (Department of Molecular Chemistry & Materials Science)
abstract: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) possess extraordinary strength and electrical conductivity. Nonetheless, CNT networks, constructed from dispersions, often suffer from inferior properties caused by nanotube bundling that limits their application in novel materials. In this talk, we will present our group’s supramolecular approach, utilizing perylene diimides (PDIs) and anthraquinones to achieve highly effective CNT dispersions in organic or aqueous solutions. We will demonstrate the application of these dispersions in the creation of robust, highly conductive buckypapers, advanced electrodes for energy materials, and transparent electrodes for next-generation flexible electronics. Ultimately, our work attempts to illustrate how mastering nanoscale interfacial chemistry provides a versatile platform for solving critical challenges in modern energy storage and transparent electronics technologies.

title: Symmetric tensor powers of octonion algebras
speaker: Aharon Razon
abstract: The fixed ring of the n-th tensor power of octonion algebras, under the action of the symmetric group, can be presented as a direct sum of central simple (non-associative) algebras. Moreover, an explicit description of this presentation is given by its central idempotents.

title: Categorification of the genus two DAHA
speaker: Daniil Sarafannikov
abstract: Arthamonov and Shakirov introduced the genus two DAHA, an algebra of operators attached to curves on a genus two surface. It contains three commuting difference operators, whose joint eigenfunctions are the genus two Macdonald polynomials. In joint work with Semeon Arthamonov and Ievgen Makedonskyi we gave an explicit realisation of these operators as functors on modules over the current algebra of a degenerate version of the Lie superalgebra D(2|1,α). The parameters q and t of the algebra keep track of two gradings on these modules, and each of the three commuting operators becomes a functor of a simple form: restrict, twist, induce. This construction also gives an explicit weight for which the genus two Macdonald polynomials are orthogonal. The talk is based on our paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13278

title: Conservativity and the big horospheric limit set for boundary actions of stationary random subgroups
speaker: Omer Segev
abstract: Let Isom(X) be the group of isometries of a proper quasiruled hyperbolic metric space X. Let µ be a probability measure on Isom(X) which generates a discrete subgroup of general type, and let µˇ be the reflected measure. Under mild assumptions, we prove that a discrete µ-stationary random subgroup almost surely has a big horospheric limit set of full measure, with respect to the µˇ-hitting measure on the Gromov boundary ∂X. We use this to deduce, under some assumptions on random walk, that the action of a stationary random subgroup of a non-elementary hyperbolic group on its Poisson boundary is conservative almost surely, and that the action of a discrete invariant random subgroups of PSL2(R) on the visual boundary of H2 is conservative. Separately, we prove that stationary random subgroups of arbitrary countable group almost surely acts conservatively on the Poisson boundary associated to the reflected random walk.

title: What Drives Trace Gas Emissions from Desert Soils: Biological, Chemical, or Biochemical Processes?
speaker: Ilya Gelfand
department: Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences
location: Seminar Room, Earth and Planetary Sciences Complex
abstract: Deserts cover nearly half of Earth’s land surface but remain among the least studied ecosystems with respect to trace gas fluxes. In particular, the processes controlling soil emissions of nitrous oxide (N₂O), nitric oxide (NO), and methane (CH₄) are still poorly understood. In this talk, I will present recent field and laboratory results exploring how coupled biotic and abiotic processes regulate these gases in arid soils, focusing on two phenomena: the CO₂, N₂O, and NO pulse following rewetting of dry soil (the “Birch effect”) and CH₄ fluxes across dry and wet seasons. Using sensitive laser-based measurements and γ-irradiated (sterilized) soils, we show that post-wetting emissions of N₂O and NO occur within minutes of rewetting and are largely driven by abiotic reactions. The results indicate that ammonium (NH₄ ) is oxidized extracellularly to hydroxylamine (NH₂OH) by released enzymes such as ammonia monooxygenase (AMO), followed by rapid abiotic oxidation of NH₂OH to N₂O. This mechanism explains the immediate N₂O pulse observed in both live and sterilized soils and underscores the overlooked role of abiotic pathways in desert N₂O production. NO is also produced, but the mechanism of its production is not yet fully understood. In parallel, we conducted nearly continuous field measurements of CH₄ fluxes using automated chambers in the Negev Desert, Israel, across soils differing in carbon content. Contrary to the prevailing view that dry soils are consistent CH₄ sinks, we found that CH₄ was emitted about 75% of the time, with mean effluxes of 0.222 ± 0.007 nmol m ² s ¹ in summer and 0.081 ± 0.004 nmol m ² s ¹ in winter. A shading experiment reduced CH₄ emissions by 51%, suggesting that solar-driven abiotic reactions, rather than microbial processes, dominate CH₄ release. Together, these findings highlight that abiotic and enzyme-mediated processes can play a major role in trace gas dynamics of arid soils, especially under the intensifying drought–rewetting cycles projected for the future climate.

title: DNA Origami comes to age: Science and applications
speaker: Prof. Yuval Garini
department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: DNA origami, invented over a decade ago, enables the construction of complex 2D and 3D nanostructures with programmable shapes. More recently, dynamic DNA origami systems have emerged, opening new opportunities in healthcare applications such as sensing, diagnostics, and targeted drug delivery. We developed a dynamic DNA origami nanocapsule for targeted drug delivery to stenotic arteries, addressing cardiovascular diseases, including atherothrombosis, which remain leading causes of death worldwide. The capsule encapsulates a clot-dissolving drug and autonomously releases it at stenotic sites in response to elevated shear forces generated by narrowed blood vessels. This approach may enable early intervention by paramedics, potentially improving current treatment strategies that rely on thrombolytic agents such as tPA, whose use is limited by bleeding risks. I will present the capsule design, synthesis, and structural characterization by AFM and electron microscopy. I will also discuss the mechanical characterization of the opening mechanism using optical tweezers.  See: H. title: On intersections of fields of rational functions
speaker: Fedor Pakovich
abstract: Fedor Pakovich (Ben Gurion U) - On intersections of fields of rational functions Let X and Y be rational functions of degree at least two with complex coefficients such that C(X,Y)=C(z). We study the problem of determining when the field C(z) is a finite extension of the intersection of C(X) and C(Y) and attains the minimal possible degree deg X * deg Y. We give a complete characterization in the case where X is a Galois covering and establish several related results.

title: Linear Hashing and Arithmetic Kakeya Sets
speaker: Or Zamir
abstract: We will introduce and study a basic question originating in computer science, without assuming any prior familiarity with the subject. Suppose we hash (that is, map) $n$ distinct integers into $m=\Theta(n)$ bins using the function $f(x) = ((ax+b) \mod p) \mod m$, where $p$ is prime and $a,b$ are chosen uniformly at random. What is the expected size of the largest bin? Despite decades of study, it remained open whether this quantity is $O(\log n/\log\log n)$, as it would be for a truly random function, or even whether it is polylogarithmic in $n$. Recently, we established an equivalence between this question and a density variant of the arithmetic Kakeya problem. In this variant, rather than requiring a set to contain an entire arithmetic progression for every common difference, we only require it to contain many points of an arithmetic progression for sufficiently many common differences. Using this equivalence and a construction of Green and Ruzsa, we obtain the first super-polylogarithmic lower bound for the maximum load of linear hashing. We will also discuss how improvements to the known upper bound would imply new results for classical arithmetic Kakeya problems.

title: The Cofinal Complexity of Ultrafilters
speaker: Tom Benhamou
abstract: We will present motivation arising from Moore-Smith convergence of nets to the study of the Tukey order restricted to ultrafilters. We will then present several long standing problems in the study of ultrafilters, tracing back to Isbell (65') and Kunen (76'), aiming to clarify how hard it is to generate/describe the cofinal structure of an ultrafilter. Also, I will lay out how my program to study the Tukey order on uncountable cardinals made progress on these problems, including a very recent theorem. Finally, some highlights from the proof will be provided, demonstrating (to some extent) the modern tools used. Only undergraduate-level set theory and very basic topology is assumed. Light refreshments will be served at 15:00 at the faculty lounge on the 8th floor.

title: Dynamical aspects of sofic and non-sofic groups
speaker: Benjamin Weiss
abstract: From their origin sofic groups have had a strong connection to topological dynamics in that it was shown that sofic groups are surjunctive - a property that is dynamical in nature. . Later on Lewis Bowen developed an entropy theory for sofic groups. This led to further extensions of dynamical invariants such as mean dimension to sofic groups. I will survey some of this history and now that it has been shown that not all groups are sofic. I will also describe some dynamical results that are valid for all countable groups.

title: Chevalley groups and their twisted analogues over rings: automorphisms and model theory
speaker: Elena Bunina
abstract:
Chevalley groups provide a common framework for classical matrix groups and exceptional groups over fields and rings. I will introduce ordinary and twisted Chevalley groups over commutative rings and discuss two related questions: how can we describe their automorphisms, and how much of the underlying ring can we recover from the group itself?

I will survey classification results for ordinary Chevalley groups and recent developments for their twisted analogues, highlighting the additional phenomena that arise in the twisted case. I will then turn to model theory, discussing the recovery of rings by first-order formulas, bi-interpretability, and consequences for elementary equivalence and axiomatizability. The emphasis will be on examples, main results, and the ideas linking the algebraic and logical approaches.

title: The two-circle trick
speaker: Orr Shalit
abstract: There is a pretty complex-geometric argument, which I call "the two-circle trick", that has come up recurrently in the classification programs of operator algebras, which allows one to replace isomorphisms by graded isomorphisms and thereby simplifies the classification. In recent work with Marcel Scherer, Eli Shamovich and Mansi Suryawanshi, this handy tool seemed to have reached its limit. I will describe what the obstacle was and how it was overcome by an unexpected application of Lie groups, giving rise to a new version of the two-circle trick. My goal in this talk is to describe this argument, starting with the operator algebraic motivation, and then stripping away the operator algebraic paraphernalia and focusing on the complex geometric essence. We shall look at one application of the trick, which is a proof that whenever two homogeneous varieties are biholomorphic, there is a biholomorphism that preserves the origin. Along the way, I hope to get across a story of how the research was done, what AI had to do with it, and how we traveled from operator algebras to several complex variables and then to Lie groups and back.

title: From Tokens to Concepts: Designing LLMs to Think More Like Humans
speaker: Chen Shani
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained to predict tokens, but humans organize and interpret the world through concepts. Can insights from human cognition help us understand and improve how LLMs represent and use knowledge? In this talk, I will explore three questions. First, do LLMs operate over human-interpretable concepts? I will examine where their conceptual representations align with human knowledge and where they fall short. Second, can explicitly modeling concepts improve LLMs? I will present approaches for incorporating concepts into training and evaluate their effects on robustness, generalization, and alignment with human judgments. Finally, how can we mathematically formulate concepts in humans and LLMs? I will discuss ways to characterize concepts at a common level of analysis, enabling more direct comparisons between human and machine cognition. Together, these questions trace a path from diagnosing how LLMs represent knowledge, through interventions to shape these representations, toward a more formal understanding of what concepts are in humans and machines. Bio Chen Shani is a Senior Lecturer at Tel Aviv University's School of Industrial & Intelligent Systems Engineering, where she leads the CoAI Lab, studying concepts, knowledge, and cognition in AI systems. Her research focuses on understanding what language models represent, how their knowledge is organized, and how these representations can be deliberately shaped. Before joining Tel Aviv University, she was a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford University and a researcher at Amazon. She holds a PhD from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

title: Faculty of Chemistry seminar
speaker: Prof. Oliver L.A. Monti
abstract: Materials for electronic devices of all kinds are dominated by a small set of materials whose properties are deeply understood and can be controlled with extraordinary precision. While the resulting electronics have arguably completely revolutionized society, there are now fundamental limitations in size, capability of integration into consumer-sized devices, and power efficiency. These limitations can only be overcome with completely new materials and device concepts, which in themselves require to go beyond charge current as information carrier. In this talk, I will introduce the notion of spin as a natural choice for low-power electronics. I will show how “small molecule” organic semiconductors can be used to tailor spintronic responses, on timescales of 10-15 s, length scales of ~10 Å and energy scales of molecular vibrations or less. Interfaces between such molecules and a wide variety of electronic materials permit conversion of charge to spin, selective spin injection or control of the spin degrees of freedom. The origin of these effects stems from the formation of a hybrid molecular interface, a chemical entity that extends beyond either the molecular material or its counterpart, enabling new ways of designing materials platforms for ultraefficient electronics.

title: Longest Alternating Subsequence in Random Pattern-Avoiding Permutations and Extensions to Longest Up/Down-Type Subsequences
speaker: Ross Pinsky
abstract: Let An(σ) denote the length of the longest alternating subsequence in a permutation σ in Sn. Under the uniform measure on Sn, this statistic was studied by Stanley. Under the uniform measure on permutations avoiding any particular pattern of length three, it was studied by Firro, Mansour and Wilson. The expected value EAn behaves asymptotically as ⅔ n in the former case and as ½ n in the latter case, regardless of which pattern of length three is to be avoided. We consider here the class of separable permutations, which is the class of permutations that can be decomposed and/or skew-decomposed down to singletons. Equivalently, it is the class of permutations that simultaneously avoid the patterns 2413 and 3142. We show that EAn ~ (2-sqrt(2)) n ≈ 0.5858 n, and also obtain the asymptotic behavior of the variance. We then consider some generalizations of alternating subsequences --- so called up/down-type subsequences. For certain choices of up/down-type subsequences, we can obtain the asymptotic behavior of the expected value of the longest such one under the uniform measure on permutations avoiding a non-monotone pattern of length three.

title: On bi-invariant geometry of free groups
speaker: Jarek Kędra
abstract: Let Fₙ denote the free group of rank n ≥ 2, equipped with the bi-invariant word metric associated with the standard generating set. I will present the following results: * Algebraic rigidity: A homomorphism Fₘ → Fₙ is a quasi-isometry if and only if it is an isomorphism. * Quasi-algebraic flexibility: There exists a quasi-homomorphism Fₘ → Fₙ which is a quasi-isometry. Consequently, asymptotic cones of non-abelian free groups of finite rank are Lipschitz isomorphic complete metric groups. Also, coarse groups associated with those bi-invariant metrics are isomorphic. * Torsion in the cone: There exist elements g ∈ F₂ such that ‖g²‖ is much smaller than ‖g‖.

title: Local Support Learning
speaker: Assaf Ben Kish
location: Lecture Hall - Room 1 - אולם הרצאות חדר 1, Jacob Ziskind Building
abstract: Modern neural networks learn in phases: large-scale pretraining followed by smaller finetuning phases. Catastrophic forgetting hurts this process, as each new phase can overwrite capabilities acquired in prior ones. First, we show that gradient updates, whether produced by SGD, Adam, or Muon, are inherently suboptimal for retaining prior capabilities. Motivated by this analysis, we propose Local Support Learning (LSL), a general-purpose learning framework that augments gradient-based training for retention of prior capabilities without access to prior data. During a new learning phase, LSL pairs two components with distinct roles: a standard weight adapter, trained as usual to minimize the loss, and a special gate based on a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) that enables the adapter only on inputs from the current phase's training distribution. Throughout multi-phase training, LSL retains 99% of prior performance while learning at full capacity, and shows favorable scaling trends in LLMs of up to 7B parameters. We complement these results with a theoretical analysis explaining why MLP-based gates are not well suited for this framework, while density estimators such as GMMs achieve near-perfect retention.Bio:Assaf Ben-Kish is a PhD student at Tel Aviv University, interested in understanding the fundamentals of learning. His work investigates deep neural networks, drawing inspiration from biological learning systems. Assaf is advised by Prof. Raja Giryes and is currently also a research intern at NVIDIA. Previously, he was a visiting student researcher in the Spoken Language Systems group at MIT CSAIL.

title: The View from Infinity: Boundaries in Large-Scale Geometry
speaker: Aditya De Saha
abstract: Gromov introduced his notion of visual boundary in his 1987 essay on hyperbolic groups. Since then, boundaries have become one of the main tools for studying spaces and groups at large scale. In this talk I will survey some of the different notions of boundaries, and why they might be interesting. In many cases a coarse invariant of the space can be computed from the boundary: Bestvina and Mess showed this for group cohomology, and Buyalo and Lebedeva for asymptotic dimension. Thomas Weighill showed that coarse homotopy groups of metric cones are the homotopy groups the base itself. I will explain a similar result (in preparation) for the Lusternik–Schnirelmann category, when the boundary is an ANR. If time permits, we will discuss the Higson corona, which is the "Universal Boundary" in a sense, and how it's algebra gives us asymptotic dimension. The talk is expository and no background in coarse geometry is assumed.

title: The Formal Verification AI Flywheel: From Productivity at Scale to Proof Power
speaker: Ziyad Hanna (Cadence)

title: On the isotropic boundary of the ample cone of a hyperkähler manifold
speaker: Amerik Ekaterina
abstract: It follows from an old result of Kovacs that the ample cone of a projective K3 surface of Picard number at least three is either“round” (equal to the positive cone), or has “no round part”, that isthe boundary of the ample cone does not contain any open subset of the isotropic cone (and is actually nowhere dense in the isotropic cone).With the help of hyperbolic geometry, this easily generalizes to the hyperkähler case.We pursue this a bit further and prove that any real analytic curve in the projectivization of the isotropic boundary of the ample cone of a projective hyperkähler manifold lies in a sphere contained in this isotropic boundary.We discuss how the union of maximal such spheres, the “Apollonian carpet”, equal to the union of all analytic curves on the projectivized isotropic boundary, can loo like.Actually, the phenomena discussed are already visible in the world of K3 surfaces; we provide some K3 examples.

title: Adapting the Lanczos algorithm to matrices with almost continuous spectra
speaker: Vladimir Druskin
abstract: We consider the approximation of multiple-input multiple-output transfer (MIMO) transfer functions of large Hermitian matrices as well as the state solution of corresponding dynamical systems. We are interested in the case with almost continuous (dense) spectrum, i.e. its eigenvalues fill one or more intervals so densely that a Krylov method cannot resolve them individually. Our target application is computations for large-scale discretizations of problems with continuous spectral measures, such as linear time-invariant PDEs on unbounded domains. Traditional Krylov methods, such as Lanczos or conjugate gradients, focus on resolving individual eigenvalues of a dense discretization, while ignoring the underlying continuous spectral measure that these points approximate. We argue that it is more efficient to model the inherent branch cut of the original operator than to exhaustively resolve the artificial point spectrum induced by discretization. For that purpose we adapt the framework of Kreĭn--Nudelman semi-infinite strings to the block Lanczos algorithm, with parameters chosen adaptively by maximizing the energy absorbed at the string termination relative to the energy stored in the string. We demonstrate significant error reductions for large-scale self-adjoint PDE discretizations in unbounded domains, including two- and three-dimensional Maxwell's equations in diffusive regimes. The method proves particularly advantageous in computing state-space solutions for wave propagation, specifically for 2D wave and 3D Maxwell operators. Implicitly replacing the conventional Lanczos spectral decomposition with a representation in terms of the continuous Kreĭn--Nudelman spectrum, we obtain a qualitative improvement in finite-difference approximations, effectively transforming standing-wave artifacts into outgoing propagating waves.

title: Random walks on the Hamiltonian diffeomorphism group
speaker: Adrian Dawid
location: Zoom session and screening in Schreiber 309, Tel Aviv University
abstract: What is a random Hamiltonian diffeomorphism? In this talk, we propose an answer by constructing a family of probability measures on the group $\mathrm{Ham}(M)$ of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms of a closed symplectic manifold $M$. We outline the construction, which is based on Gaussian processes. We then use these measures to obtain irreducible random walks on $\mathrm{Ham}(M)$. These random walks can be used to probe the large-scale geometry of $\mathrm{Ham}(M)$ with respect to the Hofer metric. On complex projective space $\mathbb{C} P^n$, we will see that the expected Hofer distance of the random walk from the identity grows at least as fast as the square root of the number of steps. By contrast, when the random walk is restricted to a commutative subgroup, the expected Hofer distance cannot grow faster than the square root of the number of steps. We conclude by showing that these bounds agree for the random walk restricted to the subgroup of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms that admit $\mathbb{T}^n$-invariant Hamiltonian functions.

title: Physics Colloquium : "The optics of life - The materials and physics behind biogenic structural colors and its biomimetics"
speaker: Dan Oron, Weizmann
location: Place:     Levin building, Lecture Hall No. 8
abstract: Light is the source of life on Earth, and is used in numerous ways in the plant and animal kingdoms for a variety of applications, including photosynthesis, vision, camouflage, communication, thermal management and more. As such, evolution has led to the creation of intricate optical systems with highly controlled and regulated properties. The talk will present an overview of some of these unique optical systems, focusing on the ubiquitous guanine-based optical reflectors and on more recently discovered 3D structural color systems. In particular, correlated optical and structural characterization will be shown to unearth new information about the function of some of the more poorly understood biological light manipulation systems and to reveal clues about their evolution. Finally, the potential for previously unexplored bioinspired optics based on these findings will be discussed.

title: A CURIOUS CASE OF PNICTOGEN CATIONS
speaker: Prof. Roman Dobrovetsky
affiliation: School of Chemistry, Tel Aviv University, Israel
abstract: Group 15 species have attracted considerable attention for their potential to activate small molecules and mediate catalytic transformations. In particular, structurally constrained pnictogen centers have emerged as promising platforms for transition-metal-like reactivity. Our research focuses on structurally constrained Pn(III) and Pn(V) cations (Pn = pnictogen), which exhibit distinct but complementary reactivity patterns. As we have recently demonstrated for P(III) systems, structural constraint can promote ambiphilic small-molecule activation and transition-metal-mimicking catalysis. In contrast, P(V) cations can exhibit exceptional Lewis acidity, enabling small-molecule activation and catalytic transformations. In this talk, I will highlight the potential of structurally constrained pnictogen cations as versatile platforms for small-molecule activation and catalysis, presenting recent advances in the chemistry of these species. These include H2 activation and metallomimetic catalytic hydrogenation mediated by constrained P(III) cations, C–Si bond activation by a structurally constrained Sb(III) cation followed by catalytic silane redistribution, and the development of novel P(V)-based Lewis superacids and their reactivity toward small molecules.

title: KnOLS: Classical Linear Regression to the Dimensional Limit- and Beyond
speaker: Iman Jaljuli
abstract: High-dimensional linear regression with correlated predictors remains challenging for statistical inference, even when the sample size is slightly greater than the number of predictors. Although substantial progress has been made in variable selection and false discovery rate (FDR) control, including through knockoff-filter (KF) methods, two important gaps remain: (1) parametric effect-size inference, including confidence intervals and type I error control (2) effective inference when signals are extremely sparse, with only a handful of predictors associated with the outcome. We develop KnOLS, an inferential framework for high-dimensional linear regression with correlated predictors, particularly when 𝑛≤𝑝 or 𝑛 only slightly exceeds 𝑝. Our approach repurposes knockoffs, traditionally used for variable selection in KF models, to reconstruct classical linear-model inferential statistics when standard methods are inapplicable. Exploiting knockoff structure, we obtain unbiased effect estimators, valid confidence intervals, and exact 𝑝-values under Gaussian errors. Unlike existing high-dimensional approaches, our framework requires no sparsity assumptions, prior structural information, or tuning parameters, and accommodates both low-dimensional (p<n) and high-dimensional (p\gg n) settings with Fixed-X and Model-X knockoffs. Simulation studies demonstrate accurate type I error control and power competitive with ordinary least squares (OLS) in low-dimensional settings. This advantage is particularly prominent when n slightly exceeds p, where OLS applies but loses power, and when 𝑛≤𝑝 and signals are extremely sparse, where the KF can exhibit down to zero power. To our knowledge, this framework provides the first end-to-end frequentist parametric approach to effect-size inference in correlated high-dimensional linear regression.

title: Network-driven discovery of therapeutics targeting the hallmarks of aging
speaker: Bnaya Gross
abstract: Despite the thousands of genes implicated in age-related phenotypes, effective interventions for aging remain elusive due to the multifactorial nature of longevity and the interconnectedness of molecular components involved. Network medicine addresses this complexity using mathematical and computational approaches rooted in network science, mapping disease-associated genes onto the human interactome, the network of physical interactions between proteins, to identify potential therapeutics. It has shown that disease genes cluster into identifiable network modules, and that a drug’s therapeutic potential can be predicted by quantifying its network proximity to those modules [1–3]. In a recent study [4], we applied this framework to aging. We mapped 2,358 longevity-associated genes onto the human interactome and found that the genes linked to each hallmark of aging [5] form a connected subgraph, or hallmark module. This allowed us to quantify the network proximity of 6,442 compounds to each hallmark using graph-based measures. We then introduced pAGE, a transcription-based metric that quantifies whether drug-induced expression changes reinforce or counteract the known age-related expression changes within each hallmark module. Combining network proximity with pAGE, we developed a quantitative framework to identify repurposable drug candidates for specific hallmarks of aging. The framework is falsifiable and interpretable, revealing the molecular mechanisms through which drugs modulate each hallmark. Finally, I will present our ongoing extension of this framework to dietary interventions. Food contains thousands of bioactive compounds with largely unmapped effects on human biology. Applying the same network-based approach, we identify food-derived compounds that may modulate the hallmarks of aging. I will conclude by discussing how mathematical modeling and network-based methods can connect genomic discoveries to therapeutics, from approved drugs to everyday nutrition, and open new directions for aging research. References 1. Barabási, A.-L., Gulbahce, N. & Loscalzo, J. Network medicine: a network-based approach to human disease. Nat. Rev. Genet. 12, 56–68 (2011). 2. Science, 347(6224), 1257601. 3. Guney, E., Menche, J., Vidal, M., & Barábasi, A. L. (2016). Network-based in silico drug efficacy screening. Nature communications, 7(1), 10331. 4. title: Central Limit Theorems for Finitary Factors of iid Processes
speaker: Nicolò Paviato
abstract:
Given a Z^d-subshift with an invariant probability measure, we study statistical limit theorems for the Birkhoff sums of regular observables. Although the literature for d = 1 is well developed, for Z^d-actions with d ≥ 2 the theory is much less understood. In this talk, we present our techniques to study such systems under the assumption that they are finitary factors of iid processes with suitable coding radius estimates. We prove a central limit theorem with rates of convergence and a functional limit theorem with a Brownian-sheet limit. Our results can be applied to classical models in statistical mechanics, such as the Ising model, proper colourings, and the hard-core model, among others.

This is joint work with Prof. Zemer Kosloff and Prof. Raimundo Briceño.

title: Spatial self-organization and oxygen field dynamics of multispecies aerobic bacteria
speaker: Prof. Joel Stavans
affiliation: Department of Physics of Complex Systems, Weizmann Institute
department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: The appearance of oxygen on Earth following the Great Oxygenation Event 2.4 Gya ago and its gradual rise to modern levels brought profound changes on extant life and its spatial organization. This is true of bacterial communities in various ecosystems, from soil, sediments and microbial mats, to the fresh-water column and the oceans. Oxytactic motile bacteria swim following oxygen gradients, and in suspension near a air-liquid interface can drive self-organized, collective coherent flows called bioconvection, whose spatial scales exceed the cell size by orders of magnitude. I will present results of bioconvection experiments with multispecies suspensions of wild-type bacteria collected from the pristine hyper-diverse bacterial communities of Cuatro Ciénegas, Coahuila, Mexico, whose origin dates back to the pre-Cambrian. Our results demonstrate a plethora of amazing dynamical behaviors, including spatial segregation between different species. This segregation takes place despite enhanced mixing by the hydrodynamic flow and in the absence of antagonistic interactions between species. Using space-resolved optical oxygen detection methods, we visualized the oxygen field directly for the first time, shedding light on the tight interplay between oxygen gradients and local bacterial concentrations. Furthermore, we modulated the oxygen concentration in the air above air-water interfaces and demonstrate the fundamental role this parameter plays in setting the behavior of bioconvection, and in the auto-organization of different bacterial species, as a function of distance from the interface. The combination of oxygen consumption and preference between species is key to understanding the high diversity of species-dependent bioconvective patterns, dynamical  spatial segregation in suspensions, as well as the self-organization of species in the aerobic sector of microbial mats. Theoretical modelling recapitulates differences in bioconvective patterns among species and provides support for a mechanism behind segregation. abstract: In this talk some recent developments on matrix distributions and their connection to absorption times of inhomogeneous Markov processes will be discussed, in particular how and why such constructions are natural tools for modelling in non-life and life insurance applications. We illustrate the approach for the modelling of mortality in both a single- and multi-population context, as well as modelling of joint lifetimes of couples. Finally, it is shown how certain extensions to the non-Markovian case involve fractional calculus and lead to matrix Mittag-Leffler distributions, which turn out to be a flexible and parsimonious class for the modelling of large but rare insurance loss events.

department: 2026-2027 Spotlight on Science Seminar Series - Dr. Vyacheslav (Slava) Kalchenko (Department of Veterinary Resources)
abstract: An idea, a test tube, an animal experiment, a patient. That journey usually takes years. Our center helps make it possible faster. Part of my work is building optical imaging systems to study blood flow in the brain and help doctors monitor skin grafts in the clinic. Now AI is changing the pace of our work. A year of software development can now take a week, sometimes only a day. Ideas arrive faster than we can test them. Could computer simulations help us keep up? From 3D-printed tools for experiments to virtual physiology and even simulations in computational psychiatry, I will share what surprised us, where simulation can spare animals, and where it cannot. Can our ability to test keep pace with our ability to create? It can, with the right crew.

title: Restoring the balance: mechanics of differentiation and regeneration in the mammalian inner ear
speaker: Prof. David Sprinzak
department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: The mammalian hearing and balance systems rely on specialized sensory hair cells that convert sound waves and head movements to electrical signals in our brain. These hairs cells are located within sensory domains where each sensory hair cell is surrounded by non-sensory supporting cells, forming a checkerboard-like pattern. Many non-mammalian species like fish and birds have the capability to regenerate lost hair cells by the proliferation and differentiation of nearby supporting cells. In contrast, in mammals the capacity to regenerate hair cells exists at early postnatal stage, but quickly diminishes after birth. Little is known about the local factors underlying the decision to trans-differentiate and the reasons for the decline in regeneration capacity with age. We combine live imaging of mouse inner ear explants and biophysical modelling to elucidate the local signaling and mechanical cues that regulate differentiation and regeneration of hair cells. We reveal unexpected age-dependent dynamic patterning processes that deviate from the classical models describing the differentiation of hair cells and supporting cells. We find that mechanical stress in the sensory domains changes with age and that perturbing it alters the observed differentiation patterns. A biophysical model incorporating local mechanical regulation of intercellular signaling captures both hair cell differentiation and regeneration patterns across ages. Together, these findings identify mechanical stress as a crucial regulator of hair cell differentiation and support an underlying mechanism in which the interplay between local mechanics and signaling shapes regenerative responses. This coupling offers a framework for understanding the age-dependent decline in hair cell regeneration and motivates investigation of mechanical regulation as a potential therapeutic target for hearing and balance disorders. title: Every Layer Counts: An Exponential L₂ Depth Hierarchy for ReLU Networks.
speaker: Itai Safran
abstract: Depth can provably increase the expressive power of neural networks: functions represented efficiently by deeper networks may require exponentially larger networks at smaller depths. For ReLU networks, however, previous exponential separations were confined to depth 2 versus depth 3 and the “deep versus very deep” regime, where the gap between the competing depths grows with the problem parameters. Whether a single additional layer can provide an exponential advantage at every fixed depth remained open. In this talk, I will present an exponential depth hierarchy for ReLU networks in which every additional layer can save exponentially many neurons. For every fixed k ≥ 2, we construct a globally [0,1]-valued, 1-Lipschitz function realized by a depth-(k+1) network of width O(d⁴), whereas approximating it at depth k to sufficiently small constant L₂ error requires width exponential in the input dimension, even with unrestricted weights. This establishes the first exponential hierarchy across all adjacent fixed depths. Short bio: Itay is a Senior Lecturer (Assistant Professor) at the Faculty of Computer and Information Science at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. His research focuses on theoretical machine learning, with an emphasis on deep learning theory. His work explores the intersection of deep learning theory with related fields, including approximation theory, optimization, and theoretical computer science.

title: Good Karma: The Computational Lens and Society
speaker: Prof. Omer Reingold
abstract: As computation changes how we live, work, and make decisions about one another, understanding and helping shape its societal impact is part of the professional responsibility of theoretical computer scientists. This responsibility extends across the many areas our field touches and a multitude of societal concerns. We also have something powerful to contribute: the computational lens often transforms our understanding of long-standing notions such as secrecy, knowledge, privacy, fairness, and incentives. Theory helps us formulate difficult questions, uncover hidden obstacles, and discover new possibilities. Sometimes this work comes with a pleasant bonus: deep theory and applications we had no idea we were looking for. Call it good karma. We will explore this exchange through algorithmic fairness. How can we make predictions that serve people well across the many overlapping groups they belong to? Following this question has led to ideas such as multicalibration and outcome indistinguishability, connecting fairness to learning, statistics, and complexity theory. Along the way, efforts to address discrimination have shed light on the meaning of individual probabilities and produced new approaches to robust learning with uses well beyond fairness. We will then turn to the foundations of AI alignment. How can we train and supervise systems whose capabilities may exceed our ability to evaluate their work? Here, even finding the right questions requires substantial creativity. The experience with cryptography, privacy, computational game theory and algorithmic fairness offers reasons to take on this challenge with ambition. We can also expect that, by doing work that matters, we will also discover deep theory we did not know we were missing.

title: A self-organized compression network arrests epithelial proliferation
speaker: Dr. Lior Attia
affiliation: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Ben-Gurion University
department: The Clore Center for Biological Physics
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Physics Library
abstract: As epithelial development or wound closure approaches completion, cell proliferation progressively slows via contact inhibition of proliferation (CIP)—a mechanism understood as being strictly local. Here we report the discovery of inhibition of proliferation through an unanticipated mechanism that is non-local. As a confluent epithelial layer becomes progressively more jammed, two interpenetrating networks emerge: islands of mechanically compressed non-cycling cells growing within an ocean of mechanically tensed cycling cells. The evolution of the compression network was found to be susceptible to both specific molecular stimuli and injury-induced unjamming. Interestingly, despite these perturbations, the size distribution of compressed islands consistently followed a power law with a cutoff that shifted toward larger island sizes as the network developed. This behavior was accompanied by a characteristic length scale that diverged as the system approached, but never crossed, the percolation threshold. These features were well captured by preferential network simulations. Together, these findings demonstrate the existence of a network-based inhibition of proliferation (NIP) that is self-organizing and poised in proximity to criticality. Finally, I will discuss emerging directions aimed at uncovering the mechanical origins of intracellular compression and how local cell divisions and mechanical interactions drive the self-organization of compressed-cell networks.

title: Self-Play Pretraining with Zero Data
speaker: Yoav Levine
abstract: Advances in language modeling have been driven by scaling pretraining on ever more data. Yet, the training data is still largely curated on the model's behalf. A more general approach to pretraining would let the model learn to generate the data most useful for its own improvement. This would provide an effectively unbounded source of training data, limited by compute rather than human knowledge. We introduce Self-Play Pretraining with Zero Data, an initial proof-of-concept towards realizing this vision. Our procedure casts synthetic data generation as a search over the space of all computable structure, taking inspiration from Solomonoff induction. Starting from random initialization, two models learn in tandem: a generator proposes programs interpreted by a universal Turing machine, generating byte sequences, while a learner autoregressively predicts these byte sequences. The learner is trained with standard cross-entropy, while the generator is trained with reinforcement learning to produce sequences at the frontier of the learner's capabilities, yielding an adaptive curriculum. A universal Turing machine gives us a search space over all computable data-generating processes, imposing little domain-specific structure, and self-play searches over this space for useful training data. We test whether zero-shot performance on natural data improves predictably with self-play compute; this is a clean test of transfer since neither generator nor learner is trained on natural data. Across several natural datasets, zero-shot loss exhibits predictable scaling in compute. The models also exhibit in-context learning, and discover recognizable mathematical sequences during training.

title: Rigidity of integrability for the Toda lattice
speaker: Daniel Tsodikovich
abstract: The Toda lattice is a Hamiltonian system that describe the motion of n particles on a line, that interact according to an exponential nearest neighbor interaction law. This system is integrable, that is, the phase space is foliated by invariant tori, on which the flow is given by linear motion. We study deformations of the Toda lattice, where the exponential interaction law is replaced with other interaction laws. We show that a certain class of such deformations will break the integrability property. The proof relies on analysis of the orbits for high energy. Such orbits approximate the billiard dynamics in polytopes, which enables better understanding of orbits of the system. This is a joint work with Vadim Kaloshin and Illya Koval.

title: Physiological Invariance: Lessons from Excitability

abstract: An excitable cell produces a stereotyped electrical response reliably over long periods, while the molecular composition that realizes this response varies widely between cells and, over time, within each cell. Because its biophysics, biochemistry, mathematics, and physiological function are comparatively well understood, excitability offers a model system for studying such invariance.
